column3: Sets a contrary frame: wealth can become punishment rather than a cleansing means.
Adds return, disclosure, and accounting for deeds after the present action.
Supplies a contrary case in which hearts are not purified despite religious speech.
Only echoes the closing divine hearing and knowing without extending the giving scene.
Clarifies that inability to spend is not itself blameworthy when loyalty is sound.
Adds the tranquility dimension that the focus associates with the messenger's prayer.
Repeats the earlier warning that wealth may be punitive, adding little beyond 9:85.
Contrasts expenditure received as a burden with the focus's restorative transfer.
Offers a distant purity and relational-order analogy, not a giving or prayer case.
Links reverence to goodness and repair, but only indirectly to the focus.
Sets a nearby impurity boundary where speech and oaths do not restore standing.
Provides the stark contrary of refusing both confirmation and prayer.
Makes the aftereffect of charity decisive: harm can undo its relational good.
Return into infirm age does not clarify this charity, purification, or prayer.
Warns that prayer can fail in its ethical relation to others, but remains general.
Gives deference before God and messenger, not a specific contribution to 9:103.
Further distinguishes constrained non-spenders from culpable refusal.
The attempt to seize a messenger does not illuminate the focus's taking of charity.
Identifies a known due within wealth, grounding a distributive side of giving.
Directly joins expenditure as nearness with the messenger's prayers and mercy.
Offers a limited analogy about taking wealth under a binding relationship.
Military return and expulsion do not add to the focus.
Its mixed good and bad work supplies the immediate condition that cleansing addresses.
Settlement after displacement is unrelated to the focus's transfer and prayer.
Places almsgiving and prayer within a broad pattern of faithful, righteous practice.
The return-and-restoration pattern is only a remote parallel to the focus's reassurance.
Connects purification with flourishing, extending the stated purpose of the gift.
Specifies that charities have ordered recipients and an assigned social distribution.
Contrasts the genuinely unable with those affluent enough to act but seeking exemption.
Shows communal prayer as a participatory relation, though not the focus's individual address.
Combines charity, purification, speech, and an inability exception in a close parallel.
Adds the nearby process in which claimed excuses are tested by subsequent work.
Purity of access is only a distant and qualified analogy to cleansing persons.
The auxiliary calm/rest reading is too general to add beyond the focus's reassurance.
Develops cleansing as a sustained communal practice tied to a sound foundation.
Adds a divine-prayer and mercy frame for movement from darkness, distinct from human prayer.
Supplies a contrary use of wealth that obstructs rather than approaches God.
Return to an appointed destination does not clarify 9:103.
Directly links giving one's wealth with self-purification and examines motives that can corrupt it.
Adds the prohibition on boast and injury after spending, preserving its relational benefit.
Shows that requested human satisfaction cannot override divine judgment of corrupt conduct.
Makes prayer's challenge to unrestricted control of wealth socially visible.
Purified pages offer only a remote object-to-person analogy.
Directly confirms repentance and charity as accepted by God, beyond their visible reception.
Reinforces purification as a condition of flourishing, after the more specific giving parallels.
Qualifies purification as dependent on divine grace rather than autonomous self-cleansing.
Completes the nearby return-to-report sequence by foregrounding observable work.
Prayer and mercy for the patient are a secondary parallel to the focus's reassurance.
Adds tranquility and reverence, but not the focus's giving-and-cleansing relation.
Repeats return and reporting without adding a charity or purification dimension.
Shows purification as calling for enacted devotion rather than conferring bare status.
Joins prayer, almsgiving, removal of impurity, and purification in a broader household setting.
Provides a nearby contrary setting of ignorance of divinely set limits.
Shows purification pursued under a hostile social norm, adding its cost of exclusion.
Offers an outward-cleanliness analogy that can frame purification without defining the gift.
Adds the nearby limit of hidden hypocrisy: visible knowledge is not exhaustive.
Offers only a general boundary on acquiring gains, after stronger giving evidence.
Places repentance, prayer, and almsgiving together at a boundary of restored passage.
Reinforces that wealth itself does not create nearness apart from faith and righteous work.
Pairs prayer with sacrifice, but does not further specify the focus's charitable prayer.
The battle-commitment narrative does not add to 9:103.
Provides favorable communal context but no specific cleansing or giving relation.
Sets the close contrary boundary: prayer cannot retrospectively confer belonging on persistent rejection.
Expands giving into a broad ethical pattern and names vulnerable recipients, but remains diffuse.
Contrasts cleansing with a heart-condition in which impurity increases.
Reiterates tranquility as support, adding little after 9:26.
Includes charity among ritual remedies but not the focus's cleansing relation.
Reiterates knowledge of hidden and visible, already supplied more closely by 9:105.
Mockery and sight do not add to the focus.
Regulates prayer's manner, not its cleansing or reassuring function.
Extends the nearby foundation contrast: a corrupt structure leaves enduring inner doubt.
Limits responsibility for another's purification while preserving the offered admonition.
Broadly pairs prayer and almsgiving with ethics, but adds little after prior parallels.
Questioning alone has no useful connection to 9:103.
Repeats the exclusion-for-purity pattern already supplied by 27:56.
Adds a forgiving relational posture, only indirectly relevant to taking and restoring.
Supplies the corrupt-institution contrast of harmful intent and false claims near 9:103.
Shows prayer under obstruction, but not its role following charitable cleansing.
Taking the Book firmly does not clarify the focus.
Contrasts faith by permission with impurity placed on those who refuse reason.
Purifying a worship space is a remote parallel to purifying people through charity.
The criticized ritual form does not add to the focus's prayer or charity.
Sharpens the nearby foundation contrast between reverence and collapse.
Integrates prayer, almsgiving, faith, and communal maintenance in a durable social setting.
Household support obligations do not clarify the focus's cleansing and prayer.
The reinforced prophetic covenant is too indirect despite a shared taking motif.
Connects prayer, almsgiving, and offered good, while adding a circulation-of-benefit perspective.
Sets an ethical limit on mixing others' wealth with one's own, relevant to accountable handling.
Contrasts institutional service with fuller faith and struggle, but adds little to 9:103.
Reiterates the prayer following purification already established by 87:14.
Inheritance apportionment does not illuminate 9:103.
Provides a transfer-integrity boundary: a completed wealth transfer is not simply reclaimed.
General obedience to limits adds no specific insight after earlier evidence.
The punitive taking motif is too remote from charity's restorative taking.
A demand for a sign does not clarify the focus.
Frames wealth transfer as preventing closed circulation among the rich and ties it to messenger-guided limits.
Household provision offers only a distant analogy of material responsibility.
Its conflict boundary does not add to understanding 9:103.
The prophetic covenant does not add to the focus.
Punitive seizure is unrelated to charity, cleansing, or reassurance here.
Supplies the growth logic of spending in God's path that directly deepens purification through giving.
Sets the explicit boundary that injury and self-display can nullify charity's good.
Contrasts that nullification with giving rooted in inner confirmation and productive growth.
Extends the warning against a later reversal that destroys the fruit of prior giving.
Requires the giver to select sound possessions rather than shifting inferior goods outward.
Names fear of loss as a pressure that can obstruct generous transfer.
Distinguishes public and concealed charity and connects concealed giving with expiation.
Fixes the recipient's guidance apart from the giver's God-directed intention and recompense.
Adds varied times and visible or hidden modes of sustained spending.
Explicitly opposes destructive gain to God's increase of charities.
Makes giving from what one values a measure of reaching righteousness.
Provides the contrary motive of spending for people to see rather than for God.
Pairs charity with goodness and reconciliation in speech, close to the focus's prayerful restoration.
Establishes a due within produce at harvest, extending the accountable-transfer frame.
Sets the nearby contrary of hoarded wealth withheld from God's path.
Carries that withholding into its consequence, sharpening the ethical boundary around wealth.
States that expenditure can be unaccepted, a necessary contrary to accepted charity in 9:103.
Identifies disbelief, negligent prayer, and reluctant spending as barriers to acceptance.
Adds the immediate dispute over charities and the legitimacy of their distribution.
Introduces a promise to give charity when bounty is received, setting up a nearby test of return.
Shows bounty being withheld after receipt, the direct contrary to a faithful transfer.
Traces broken giving commitments into enduring hypocrisy, complementing the mixed-work context.
Adds social contempt toward voluntary and small contributions, clarifying the reception of giving.
Frames material transfer as a due owed to kin, the needy, and the traveler.
Sets a balance between withholding and wasteful dispersal of wealth.
Directly contrasts self-serving increase with charity sought for God and its growth.
Frames wealth as entrusted succession and spending as a response to that custody.
Adds the significance of when one spends, distinguishing earlier from later costly commitment.
Returns charity to the focus's increase theme through a doubled recompense frame.
Places spending before death as a decisive missed opportunity for repair.
States that spending can be for one's own good while warning against possessive impulse.
Completes the recognized due in wealth by naming both the asking and deprived claimant.
Excludes repayment of a personal favor as the controlling motive of the giver in 92:18.
Completes that giving pattern with seeking the highest Lord's acceptance.
Supplies the contrary of withholding ordinary aid, extending prayer's ethical outcome.
Presents a voluntary transfer to God as a loan subject to multiplication.
Places spending before a final day when exchange and intercession no longer operate.
Adds a recipient profile for need that remains concealed by restraint.
Makes remission of a debt as charity a higher form of material repair.
Extends righteous giving to both ease and hardship, not merely surplus.
Sets withholding of God-given bounty as a contrary possessive posture.
Contrasts faith-linked spending with the preceding display-oriented expenditure.
Joins prayer, almsgiving, and a good loan within covenantal restoration.
Places prayer and almsgiving in a defining communal allegiance pattern.
Connects almsgiving with reverence, mercy, and faith in the signs.
Pairs established prayer with spending from provision in a compact believer profile.
Places hidden and open spending among persevering practices that repel evil.
Commands prayer and hidden or open spending before irreversible exchange ends.
Treats prayer and almsgiving as an enduring charge across a life.
Shows prayer and almsgiving being enjoined within a household and approved by God.
Links guidance, good works, prayer, and almsgiving under divine direction.
Adds spending from provision to hearts responsive to God's remembrance.
Places prayer and almsgiving among public marks of established communal capacity.
Names active performance of almsgiving as a believer characteristic.
Shows prayer and almsgiving retained despite commerce and fear of final accounting.
Pairs prayer and almsgiving with obedience in pursuit of mercy.
Uses prayer and almsgiving as a concise profile alongside certainty in the hereafter.
Repeats that profile in a wisdom-and-guidance setting, adding little but relevant support.
Places charitable men and women among parallel forms of faithful discipline.
Combines recitation, prayer, and hidden or open spending as a non-failing transaction.
Sets refusal of almsgiving beside denial of the hereafter as a severe contrary profile.
Exposes miserliness as self-directed loss when called to spend in God's path.
Adds the removal of the prior charity requirement while retaining prayer, almsgiving, and obedience.
Condenses upright religion into devotion, prayer, and almsgiving.
